However, during periods of enteric Escherichia coli challenge, results have been inconsistent. Here, we investigated whether independent or combined arginine and glutamine supplementation could improve performance and immune response under an E.

studies.title: L-Glutamine is better for treatment than prevention in exhaustive exercise.
studies.abstract: Introduction: Glutamine is known as the richest nonessential amino acid in the human body. The intake of glutamine is not only beneficial to nutrition but also reported to enhance inflammation reducing bioactivity in exercise. Although studies have demonstrated that glutamine is beneficial for exercise, the optimal intake timing remains unclear. This study examined whether the effects of glutamine on tissue damage and physiology differ between intake timings. Methods: Rats were divided into without L-glutamine supplementation (vehicle), with L-glutamine before exhaustive exercise (prevention), and with L-glutamine after exhaustive exercise (treatment) groups. Exhaustive exercise was induced by treadmill running and L-glutamine was given by oral feeding. The exhaustive exercise began at a speed of 10 miles/min and increased in increments of 1 mile/min, to a maximum running speed of 15 miles/min with no incline. The blood samples were collected before exhaustive exercise, 12 h and 24 h after exercise to compare the creatine kinase isozyme MM (CK-MM), red blood cell count and platelet count. The animals were euthanized on 24 h after exercise, and tissue samples were collected for pathological examination and scored the severity of organ injury from 0 to 4. Results: The CK-MM was elevated gradually after exercise in the vehicle group; however, CK-MM was decreased after L-glutamine supplementation in the treatment group. The treatment group had higher red blood cell count and platelet count than the vehicle and prevention group after exercise. In addition, the treatment group had less tissue injury in the cardiac muscles, and kidneys than prevention group. Conclusion: The therapeutic effect of L-glutamine after exhaustive exercise was more effective than preventive before exercise.

studies.title: Long-Term L-Glutamine Treatment Reduces Hemolysis without Ameliorating Hepatic Vaso-Occlusion and Liver Fibrosis in a Mouse Model of Sickle Cell Disease.
studies.abstract: Sickle cell disease (SCD) is an autosomal recessive monogenic disorder caused by a homozygous mutation in the β-globin gene, which leads to erythrocyte sickling, hemolysis, vaso-occlusion, and sterile inflammation. The administration of oral L-glutamine has been shown to reduce the frequency of pain in SCD patients; however, the long-term effect of L-glutamine in SCD remains to be determined. To understand the long-term effect of L-glutamine administration in the liver we used quantitative liver intravital microscopy and biochemical analysis in humanized SCD mice. We here show that chronic L-glutamine administration reduces hepatic hemoglobin-heme-iron levels but fails to ameliorate ischemic liver injury. Remarkably, we found that this failure in the resolution of hepatobiliary injury and persistent liver fibrosis is associated with the reduced expression of hepatic Kupffer cells post-L-glutamine treatment. These findings establish the importance of investigating the long-term effects of L-glutamine therapy on liver pathophysiology in SCD patients.

studies.title: L-Glutamine and Physical Exercise Prevent Intestinal Inflammation and Oxidative Stress Without Improving Gastric Dysmotility in Rats with Ulcerative Colitis.
studies.abstract: The aim of this study was to evaluate the effects of glutamine supplementation or exercise on gastric emptying and intestinal inflammation in rats with ulcerative colitis (UC). Strength exercise consisted of jump training 4 × 10 repetitions/5 days a week/8 weeks with progressive overload. Endurance exercise consisted of swimming without overload for a period of 1 h a day/5 days a week/8 weeks. Another group (sedentary) of animals was supplemented with L-glutamine (1 g/kg of body weight) orally for 8 weeks before induction of UC. Colitis was induced by intra-colonic administration of 1 mL of 4% acetic acid. We assessed gastric emptying, macroscopic and microscopic scoring, oxidative stress markers, and IL-1β, IL-6, and (TNF-α) levels. The UC significantly increased (p < 0.05) the gastric emptying compared with the saline control group. We observed a significantly decrease (p < 0.05) in body weight gain in UC rats compared with the control groups. Both exercise interventions and L-glutamine supplementation significantly prevented (p < 0.05) weight loss compared with the UC group. Strength and endurance exercises significantly prevented (p < 0.05) the increase of microscopic scores and oxidative stress (p < 0.05). L-glutamine supplementation in UC rats prevented hemorrhagic damage and improved oxidative stress markers (p < 0.05). Strength and endurance exercises and glutamine decreased the concentrations of inflammatory cytokines IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α compared with the UC group (p < 0.05). Strength and endurance exercises and L-glutamine supplementation prevented intestinal inflammation and improved cytokines and oxidative stress levels without altering gastric dysmotility in rats with UC.

studies.title: Oral Glutamine Supplementation Reduces Obesity, Pro-Inflammatory Markers, and Improves Insulin Sensitivity in DIO Wistar Rats and Reduces Waist Circumference in
studies.abstract: In the present study, we aimed to investigate whether chronic oral glutamine (Gln) supplementation may alter metabolic parameters and the inflammatory profile in overweight and obese humans as well as whether Gln may modulate molecular pathways in key tissues linked to the insulin action in rats. Thirty-nine overweight/obese volunteers received 30 g of Gln or alanine (Ala-control) for 14 days. Body weight (BW), waist circumference (WC), hormones, and pro-inflammatory markers were evaluated. To investigate molecular mechanisms, Gln or Ala was given to Wistar rats on a high-fat diet (HFD), and metabolic parameters, euglycemic hyperinsulinemic clamp with tracers, and Western blot were done. Gln reduced WC and serum lipopolysaccharide (LPS) in overweight volunteers. In the obese group, Gln diminished WC and serum insulin. There was a positive correlation between the reduction on WC and LPS. In rats on HFD, Gln reduced adiposity, improved insulin action and signaling, and reversed both defects in glucose metabolism in the liver and muscle. Gln supplementation increased muscle glucose uptake and reversed the increased hepatic glucose production, in parallel with a reduced glucose uptake in adipose tissue. This insulin resistance in AT was accompanied by enhanced IRS1 O-linked-glycosamine association in this tissue, but not in the liver and muscle. These data suggest that Gln supplementation leads to insulin resistance specifically in adipose tissue via the hexosamine pathway and reduces adipose mass, which is associated with improvement in the systemic insulin action. Thus, further investigation with Gln supplementation should be performed for longer periods in humans before prescribing as a beneficial therapeutic approach for individuals who are overweight and obese.

studies.title: Does l-glutamine-supplemented diet extenuate NO-mediated damage on myenteric plexus of Walker 256 tumor-bearing rats?
studies.abstract: This study was designed to appraise the relationship between enteric neuropathy and oxidative stress in cancer cachexia under l-glutamine-supplemented diet. Total and nitrergic neuronal populations were investigated in jejunum and ileum in four experimental groups: control (C); control l-glutamine-supplemented diet (CG); Walker-256 tumor (TW); and Walker-256 tumor supplemented with l-glutamine (TWG). In addition, local oxidative stress, neuronal nitric oxide synthase (nNOS) enzyme and nitric oxide (NO) levels were evaluated. Neuronal density and somatic area of the total and nitrergic populations were reduced in TW rats, which was accompanied by high oxidative stress, NO and nNOS levels. l-glutamine supplementation prevented neuronal atrophy, changes in pan neuronal density and nNOS overexpression (ileum), and restored total antioxidant capacity. Nevertheless, the oxidative stress was partially mitigated and no effect was observed on the reduction of nitrergic population and NO levels. l-glutamine-supplemented diet extenuates NO-mediated damage on the myenteric plexus although has a small benefit on oxidative stress.

studies.title: Experimental Cancer Cachexia Changes Neuron Numbers and Peptide Levels in the Intestine: Partial Protective Effects after Dietary Supplementation with L-Glutami
studies.abstract: Gastrointestinal dysmotility frequently occurs in cancer cachexia and may result from damage to enteric innervation caused by oxidative stress, especially due to glutathione depletion. We assessed the effect of dietary supplementation with 20 g/kg l-glutamine (a glutathione precursor) on the intrinsic innervation of the enteric nervous system in healthy and Walker 256 tumor-bearing Wistar rats during the development of experimental cachexia (14 days), in comparison with non-supplemented rats, by using immunohistochemical methods and Western blotting. The total neural population and cholinergic subpopulation densities in the myenteric plexus, as well as the total population and VIPergic subpopulation in the submucosal plexus of the jejunum and ileum, were reduced in cachectic rats, resulting in adaptive morphometric alterations and an increase in vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) and calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) expression, suggesting a neuroplastic response. l-glutamine supplementation prevented decrease in myenteric neuronal density in the ileum, morphometric alterations in the neurons and nerve fibers (in both the plexuses of the jejunum and ileum), and the overexpression of VIP and CGRP. Cancer cachexia severely affected the intrinsic innervation of the jejunum and ileum to various degrees and this injury seems to be associated with adaptive neural plasticity. l-glutamine supplementation presented partial protective effects on the enteric innervation against cancer cachexia, possibly by attenuating oxidative stress.

studies.title: Dietary L-glutamine supplementation modulates microbial community and activates innate immunity in the mouse intestine.
studies.abstract: This study was conducted to determine effects of dietary supplementation with 1 % L-glutamine for 14 days on the abundance of intestinal bacteria and the activation of intestinal innate immunity in mice. The measured variables included (1) the abundance of Bacteroidetes, Firmicutes, Lactobacillus, Streptococcus and Bifidobacterium in the lumen of the small intestine; (2) the expression of toll-like receptors (TLRs), pro-inflammatory cytokines, and antibacterial substances secreted by Paneth cells and goblet cells in the jejunum, ileum and colon; and (3) the activation of TLR4-nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB), mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPK), and phosphoinositide-3-kinases (PI3K)/PI3K-protein kinase B (Akt) signaling pathways in the jejunum and ileum. In the jejunum, glutamine supplementation decreased the abundance of Firmicutes, while increased mRNA levels for antibacterial substances in association with the activation of NF-κB and PI3K-Akt pathways. In the ileum, glutamine supplementation induced a shift in the Firmicutes:Bacteroidetes ratio in favor of Bacteroidetes, and enhanced mRNA levels for Tlr4, pro-inflammatory cytokines, and antibacterial substances participating in NF-κB and JNK signaling pathways. These results indicate that the effects of glutamine on the intestine vary with its segments and compartments. Collectively, dietary glutamine supplementation of mice beneficially alters intestinal bacterial community and activates the innate immunity in the small intestine through NF-κB, MAPK and PI3K-Akt signaling pathways.

studies.title: L-glutamine supplementation prevents the development of experimental diabetic cardiomyopathy in streptozotocin-nicotinamide induced diabetic rats.
studies.abstract: The objective of the present investigation was to evaluate the effect of L-glutamine on cardiac myopathy in streptozotocin-nicotinamide induced diabetic rats. Diabetes was induced in overnight fasted Sprague Dawely rats by using intraperitonial injection of streptozotocin (55 mg/kg). Nicotinamide (100 mg/kg, i.p.) was administered 20 min before administration of streptozotocin. Experimental rats were divided into Group I: non-diabetic control (distilled water; 10 ml/kg, p.o.), II: diabetic control (distilled water, 10 ml/kg, p.o.), III: L-glutamine (500 mg/kg, p.o.) and IV: L-glutamine (1000 mg/kg, p.o.). All groups were diabetic except group I. The plasma glucose level, body weight, electrocardiographic abnormalities, hemodynamic changes and left ventricular contractile function, biological markers of cardiotoxicity, antioxidant markers were determined after 4 months after STZ with nicotinamide injection. Histopathological changes of heart tissue were carried out by using H and E stain. L-glutamine treatment improved the electrocardiographic, hemodynamic changes; LV contractile function; biological markers; oxidative stress parameters and histological changes in STZ induced diabetic rats. Results from the present investigation demonstrated that L-glutamine has seemed a cardioprotective activity.

studies.title: Effects of L-glutamine on rectal temperature and some markers of oxidative stress in Red Sokoto goats during the hot-dry season.
studies.abstract: The experiment investigated the ameliorative effects of L-glutamine administration on rectal temperature (RT), erythrocyte osmotic fragility (EOF), serum antioxidant enzyme activities and malondialdehyde (MDA) concentration in Red Sokoto goats during the hot-dry season. Twenty eight healthy Red Sokoto goats, comprising 14 experimental (administered 0.2 g/kg of L-glutamine dissolved in 10 mL of distilled water, once daily for 21 days) and 14 control (administered equivalent of distilled water) goats served as subjects. Rectal temperature (measured at 6:00, 13:00 and 18:00 h) and blood samples (taken at 8:00 h) were obtained from all subjects weekly, before, during and after L-glutamine administration. Data obtained were compared using one-way repeated-measures ANOVA, followed by Tukey's post-hoc test. The dry-bulb temperature, relative humidity and temperature-humidity index for the study period ranged between 24.0 and 37.5 °C, 26.0 and 84.0% and 73.0 and 86.3, respectively. L-glutamine administration decreased (P < 0.05) RT, EOF and MDA and increased superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity in experimental group, compared to controls during weeks 1, 2 and 3. Glutathione peroxidase (GPx) and catalase activities were higher (P < 0.05) in the experimental group than in the controls only during week 1 of L-glutamine administration. In conclusion, L-glutamine administration mitigated increases in RT, EOF and serum MDA concentration and enhanced serum SOD, GPx and catalase activities and may be beneficial in heat-stressed goats during the hot-dry season.

studies.title: Glutamine supplementation in cystic fibrosis: A randomized placebo-controlled trial.
studies.abstract: Pulmonary infection and malnutrition in cystic fibrosis are associated with decreased survival. Glutamine has a possible anti-microbial effect, with a specific impact against Pseudomonas aeruginosa. We aimed to test the hypothesis that oral glutamine supplementation (21 g/day) for 8 weeks in adults with cystic fibrosis would decrease pulmonary inflammation and improve clinical status. The study design was a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled study design with an iso-nitrogenous placebo. The primary analysis was intention to treat, and the primary outcome was change in induced sputum neutrophils. Thirty-nine individuals were recruited and thirty-six completed the study. Glutamine supplementation had no impact on any of the outcome measures in the intention-to-treat analysis. In the per protocol analysis, glutamine supplementation was associated with an increase in induced sputum neutrophils (P = 0.046), total cells (P = 0.03), and in Pseudomonas isolation agar colony forming units (P = 0.04) compared to placebo. There was no effect of glutamine supplementation on markers of pulmonary inflammation in the intention-to-treat analysis.

studies.title: Glutamine supplementation in cancer patients.
studies.abstract: Three series of studies investigated whether 1) glutamine deficiency occurs in tumor-bearing rats, 2) glutamine supplementation improves protein metabolism during chemotherapy in tumor-bearing rats, and 3) oral glutamine supplement improves systemic immune and gut-barrier function in patients with esophageal cancer receiving radiochemotherapy. In the animal studies, AH109A hepatoma cells or Yoshida sarcoma cells were inoculated into male Donryu rats to induce tumors. Glutamine production was measured by U-14C-glutamine infusion and the conversion of arginine to glutamine was measured by infusion of U-14C-arginine. The effect of glutamine on protein metabolism was investigated by 1-14C-leucine infusion. In the clinical study, 13 patients with esophageal cancer were randomized into two groups, control and glutamine supplemented (30 g/d), for 4 wk. Glutamine levels in plasma and skeletal muscle were decreased in tumor-bearing rats, although glutamine production and the conversion of arginine to glutamine were increased. Glutamine-supplemented total parenteral nutrition reduced whole-body protein breakdown rate during chemotherapy in tumor-bearing rats. Oral supplementation of glutamine to the patients with esophageal cancer enhanced lymphocyte mitogenic function and reduced permeability of the gut during radiochemotherapy. Glutamine depletion in host tissues occurs in tumor-bearing rats. Glutamine supplementation can attenuate loss of protein in the muscle in tumor-bearing animals and protect immune and gut-barrier function during radiochemotherapy in patients with advanced cancer.

studies.title: Parenteral glutamine supplementation improves serum albumin values in surgical cancer patients.
studies.abstract: Patients with gastric adenocarcinoma (GA) often develop malnutrition, which deteriorates after cancer surgery and negatively affects surgical outcomes. Despite being an abundant and versatile amino acid involved in the immune system and metabolic functions, glutamine levels are significantly depleted among patients who are critically ill or hypercatabolic. Therefore, this study aimed to investigate whether parenteral glutamine supplementation may improve nutritional status and surgical outcomes. This retrospective, single-center cohort study included patients with GA who underwent gastrectomy between January 2007 and June 2019. Patients were classified into either the non-glutamine or glutamine group. Propensity score matching was used to minimize the bias in patient demographics. Furthermore, the average parenteral glutamine dose from the day of surgery to postoperative day four was calculated in g/kg/day. Surgical outcomes (length of hospitalization, major complication, and mortality) and changes in lymphocyte count and serum albumin levels 7 days post-surgery were assessed in both matched groups using adjusted models. A total of 1950 patients were reviewed, among whom 522 (26.8%) received parenteral glutamine supplementation (glutamine dose ranging from 0.05 to 0.49 g/kg/day). Among the included patients, 57.2% were males, and the median age was 64.9 years. After matching, there were 478 cases in each group. No differences in surgical outcomes and changes in lymphocyte count were observed between both matched groups. The glutamine group exhibited a smaller decrease in serum albumin levels compared to the non-glutamine group (-0.6 vs. -1.1 g/dL; P < 0.001). The adjusted matched model showed that glutamine dose contributed significantly toward increasing serum albumin levels (coefficient = 0.08 per 0.1 g/day/kg increment in glutamine; 95% confidence interval: 0.04 to 0.10; P < 0.001). Perioperative parenteral glutamine supplementation had a positive dose-dependent impact on the recovery of serum albumin levels among patients with GA undergoing gastrectomy, implying that glutamine supplementation improved postoperative nutritional suppression and ameliorated stress-associated inflammation. Although glutamine supplementation was not associated with surgical outcomes, further studies should be conducted to evaluate the clinical significance of serum albumin restoration.

studies.title: l-Glutamine supplementation reduces gastrointestinal permeability and biomarkers of physiological stress in preweaning Holstein heifer calves.
studies.abstract: l-Glutamine supplementation improves gastrointestinal and immune function in dairy calves during controlled immune and stress challenges. However, it is unknown whether supplementing milk replacer (MR) with l-glutamine improves preweaning dairy calf health and welfare under production conditions. Therefore, the study objective was to evaluate the effects of supplementing MR with l-glutamine on gastrointestinal permeability, immune function, growth performance, postabsorptive metabolic biomarkers, and physiological stress response in preweaning dairy calves. In 3 repetitions, Holstein heifer calves (n = 30; 1.5 ± 0.5 d old; 37.1 ± 0.86 kg body weight) were blocked by serum total protein, body weight, and age, and provided MR (3.8 L/calf per d; 24% CP, 17% fat, 12.5% solids) supplemented with l-glutamine (GLN; 10g/kg MR powder; n = 5 calves/repetition) or nonsupplemented (NSMR; n = 5 calves/repetition). Calves were individually housed with ad libitum starter grain and water access until weaning (56.4 ± 0.5 d old). At 1 and 6 wk of age, urinary catheters were placed, and calves were orally dosed with 1 L of chromium (Cr)-EDTA. Urine samples were collected over a 24-h period for Cr output analysis as an in vivo biomarker of gastrointestinal permeability. Blood was collected on study d 1, 5, 7, 14, 21, 42, and 56 to measure white blood cell counts, cortisol, insulin, glucose, nonesterified fatty acids, serum amyloid A, haptoglobin, and neutrophil: lymphocytes. Two study intervals were used in the statistical analyses, representing greater (P1; wk 1-3) and reduced (P2; wk 4-8) enteric disease susceptibility. Data were analyzed using PROC GLIMMIX in SAS 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc.) with calf as the experimental unit. Overall, total urinary Cr output was reduced in GLN versus NSMR calves. Total Cr output was reduced at 1 wk of age in GLN versus NSMR calves, but no differences were detected at 6 wk of age. Neutrophil:lymphocyte was decreased both overall and during P2 in GLN versus NSMR calves, and neutrophil counts tended to be reduced in GLN versus NSMR calves during P2. No MR treatment differences were detected for average daily feed intake, average daily gain, body measurements, postabsorptive metabolic biomarkers, disease scores, and therapeutic treatments between GLN and NSMR calves. In summary, l-glutamine supplementation reduced gastrointestinal permeability and biomarkers of physiological stress in preweaning Holstein heifer calves.

In the jejunum, glutamine supplementation decreased the abundance of Firmicutes, while increased mRNA levels for antibacterial substances in association with the activation of NF-κB and PI3K-Akt pathways. In the ileum, glutamine supplementation induced a shift in the Firmicutes:Bacteroidetes ratio in favor of Bacteroidetes, and enhanced mRNA levels for Tlr4, pro-inflammatory cytokines, and antibacterial substances participating in NF-κB and JNK signaling pathways. These results indicate that the effects of glutamine on the intestine vary with its segments and compartments. Collectively, dietary glutamine supplementation of mice beneficially alters intestinal bacterial community and activates the innate immunity in the small intestine through NF-κB, MAPK and PI3K-Akt signaling pathways.

studies.title: Dietary L-glutamine supplementation improves pregnancy outcome in mice infected with type-2 porcine circovirus.
studies.abstract: Porcine circovirus type 2 (PCV2) causes reproductive failure in swine. As glutamine can enhance immune function in animals, this study was conducted with mice to test the hypothesis that dietary glutamine supplementation will improve pregnancy outcome in PCV2-infected dams. Beginning on day 0 of gestation, mice were fed a standard diet supplemented with 1.0% L-glutamine or 1.22% L-alanine (isonitrogenous control). All mice were infected with PCV2 (2000 TCID50) on day 10 of gestation. On day 17 of gestation, six mice from each group were euthanized to obtain maternal tissues and fetuses for hematology and histopathology tests. The remaining mice continued to receive their respective diets supplemented with 1.0% L-glutamine or 1.22% L-alanine through lactation. The PCV2 virus was present in maternal samples (serum and lung) of most mice in the control group but was not detected in the glutamine-supplemented mice. Dietary glutamine supplementation reduced abortion, decreased fetal deaths, and enhanced neonatal survival. The glutamine treatment also reduced concentrations of interleukin-6, while increasing concentrations of tumor necrosis factor-α and C-reactive protein, in the maternal serum of mice. Furthermore, glutamine supplementation attenuated microscopic lesions in maternal tissues (lung, spleen, and liver). Collectively, these results indicate that dietary glutamine supplementation is beneficial for ameliorating reproductive failure in virus-infected mice. The findings support the notion that gestating dams require adequate amounts of dietary glutamine for the optimal survival and growth of embryos, fetuses, and neonates, and have important implications for nutritional support of mammals (including swine and humans) during gestation and lactation.

studies.title: L-glutamine sensitizes Gram-positive-resistant bacteria to gentamicin killing.
studies.abstract:
Importance

Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) infection severely threatens human health due to high morbidity and mortality; it is urgent to develop novel strategies to tackle this problem. Metabolites belong to antibiotic adjuvants which improve the effect of antibiotics. Despite reports of L-glutamine being applied in antibiotic adjuvant for Gram-negative bacteria, how L-glutamine affects antibiotics against Gram-positive-resistant bacteria is still unclear. In this study, L-glutamine increases the antibacterial effect of gentamicin on MRSA, and it links to membrane permeability and pH gradient (ΔpH), resulting in uptake of more gentamicin. Of great interest, reduced reactive oxygen species (ROS) by glutathione was found under L-glutamine treatment; USA300 becomes sensitive again to gentamicin. This study not only offers deep understanding on ΔpH and ROS on bacterial resistance but also provides potential treatment solutions for targeting MRSA infection.

studies.title: What Is the Role of Nutritional Supplements in Support of Total Hip Replacement and Total Knee Replacement Surgeries? A Systematic Review.
studies.abstract: Nutritional supplements can influence outcomes for individuals undergoing major surgery, particularly in older persons whose functional reserve is limited. Accelerating recovery from total hip replacement (THR) and total knee replacement (TKR) may offer significant benefits. Therefore, we explored the role of nutritional supplements in improving recovery following THR and TKR. A systematic review was conducted to source randomized clinical trials that tested nutritional supplements in cohorts of THR or TKR patients. Our search yielded nine relevant trials. Intake of a carbohydrate-containing fluid is reported to improve insulin-like growth factor levels, reduce hunger, nausea, and length of stay, and attenuate the decrease in whole-body insulin sensitivity and endogenous glucose release. Amino acid supplementation is reported to reduce muscle atrophy and accelerate return of functional mobility. One paper reported a suppressive effect of beta-hydroxy beta-methylbutyrate, L-arginine, and L-glutamine supplementation on muscle strength loss following TKR. There is limited evidence for nutritional supplementation in THR and TKR pathways; however, the low risk profile and potential benefits to adjunctive treatment methods, such as exercise programs, suggest nutritional supplements may have a role. Optimizing nutritional status pre-operatively may help manage the surgical stress response, with a particular benefit for undernourished, frail, or elderly individuals.

studies.title: The Influence of Oral L-Glutamine Supplementation on Muscle Strength Recovery and Soreness Following Unilateral Knee Extension Eccentric Exercise.
studies.abstract: The study aimed to examine the effects that L-glutamine supplementation has on quadriceps muscle strength and soreness ratings following eccentric exercise. It was hypothesized that glutamine ingestion would quicken the recovery rate of peak force production and decrease muscle soreness ratings over a 72-hr recovery period. Sixteen healthy participants (8♀/8♂; 22 ± 4 years) volunteered in a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled crossover study. Supplement conditions consisted of isoenergetic placebo (maltodextrin, 0.6 g·kg-1·day-1) and L-glutamine (0.3 g·kg-1·day-1 + 0.3 g·kg-1·day-1 maltodextrin) ingestion once per day over 72 hr. Knee extensor peak torque at 0°, 30°, and 180° per second and muscle soreness were measured before, immediately following, 24, 48, and 72 hr posteccentric exercise. Eccentric exercise consisted of 8 sets (10 repetitions/set) of unilateral knee extension at 125% maximum concentric force with 2-min rest intervals. L-glutamine resulted in greater relative peak torque at 180°/sec both immediately after (71 ± 8% vs. 66 ± 9%), and 72 hr (91 ± 8% vs. 86 ± 7%) postexercise (all, p < .01). In men, L-glutamine produced greater (p < .01) peak torques at 30°/ sec postexercise. Men also produced greater normalized peak torques at 30°/sec (Nm/kg) in the L-glutamine condition than women (all, p < .05). In the entire sample, L-glutamine resulted in lower soreness ratings at 24 (2.8 ± 1.2 vs. 3.4 ± 1.2), 48 (2.6 ± 1.4 vs. 3.9 ± 1.2), and 72 (1.7 ± 1.2 vs. 2.9 ± 1.3) hr postexercise (p < .01). The L-glutamine supplementation resulted in faster recovery of peak torque and diminished muscle soreness following eccentric exercise. The effect of L-glutamine on muscle force recovery may be greater in men than women.

studies.title: Effect of Glutamine Supplementation on Muscular Damage Biomarkers in Professional Basketball Players.
studies.abstract: Scientific evidence supports the role of L-glutamine in improving immune function. This could suggest a possible role of L-glutamine in recovery after intense exercise. To this end, the present report aimed to study if oral L-glutamine supplementation could attenuate muscle damage in a group of players of a mainly eccentric sport discipline such as basketball. Participants (n = 12) were supplemented with 6 g/day of glutamine (G group) or placebo (P group) for 40 days in a crossover study design (20 days with glutamine + 20 days with placebo and vice versa). Blood samples were obtained at the beginning and at the end of each period and markers from exercise-induced muscle damage were determined. The glutamine supplemented group displayed significantly low values of aspartate transaminase, creatine kinase and myoglobin in blood, suggesting less muscle damage compared to the placebo. In addition, adrenocorticotropic hormone levels were lower in the glutamine supplemented group than in the placebo. As a result, the circulating cortisol levels did not increase at the end of the study in the glutamine supplemented group. Altogether, the results indicate that glutamine could help attenuate exercise-induced muscle damage in sport disciplines with predominantly eccentric actions.

studies.title: Combined Exercise Training and l-Glutamine Supplementation Enhances Both Humoral and Cellular Immune Responses after Influenza Virus Vaccination in Elderly Subj
studies.abstract:
Background

Since aging affects the immune responses against vaccination, the present study evaluated the effects of L-glutamine (Gln) supplementation in the humoral and cellular immune responses in elderly subjects, practitioners or not, of physical exercise training.

Methods

Eighty-four elderly people (aged 72.6 ± 6.1), non-practitioners (NP, n = 31), and practitioners of combined-exercise training (CET, n = 53) were submitted to Influenza virus vaccination and supplemented with Gln (0.3 g/kg of weight + 10 g of maltodextrin, groups: NP-Gln (n = 14), and CET-Gln (n = 26)), or placebo (10 g of maltodextrin, groups: NP-PL (n = 17), and CET-PL (n = 27)). Blood samples were collected pre (baseline) and 30 days post-vaccination and supplementation.

Results

Comparing with the baseline values, whereas the NP-Gln and CET-PL groups showed higher specific-IgM levels, the CET-Gln group showed higher specific-IgM and IgA levels post-vaccination. The titer rate of hemagglutination inhibition was higher in the CET-Gln, NP-PL, and NP-Gln groups post-vaccination than baseline values. The absolute number of naive and effector CD4+ T cells was higher especially in the NP-Gln and CET-Gln groups, whilst activated CD4+ T cells were higher in CET subgroups post-vaccination.

Conclusion

Our results showed that both l-glutamine supplementation and combined-exercise training can improve the immune responses to the Influenza virus vaccine in elderly subjects.

studies.title: L-Glutamine and Physical Exercise Prevent Intestinal Inflammation and Oxidative Stress Without Improving Gastric Dysmotility in Rats with Ulcerative Colitis.
studies.abstract: The aim of this study was to evaluate the effects of glutamine supplementation or exercise on gastric emptying and intestinal inflammation in rats with ulcerative colitis (UC). Strength exercise consisted of jump training 4 × 10 repetitions/5 days a week/8 weeks with progressive overload. Endurance exercise consisted of swimming without overload for a period of 1 h a day/5 days a week/8 weeks. Another group (sedentary) of animals was supplemented with L-glutamine (1 g/kg of body weight) orally for 8 weeks before induction of UC. Colitis was induced by intra-colonic administration of 1 mL of 4% acetic acid. We assessed gastric emptying, macroscopic and microscopic scoring, oxidative stress markers, and IL-1β, IL-6, and (TNF-α) levels. The UC significantly increased (p < 0.05) the gastric emptying compared with the saline control group. We observed a significantly decrease (p < 0.05) in body weight gain in UC rats compared with the control groups. Both exercise interventions and L-glutamine supplementation significantly prevented (p < 0.05) weight loss compared with the UC group. Strength and endurance exercises significantly prevented (p < 0.05) the increase of microscopic scores and oxidative stress (p < 0.05). L-glutamine supplementation in UC rats prevented hemorrhagic damage and improved oxidative stress markers (p < 0.05). Strength and endurance exercises and glutamine decreased the concentrations of inflammatory cytokines IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α compared with the UC group (p < 0.05). Strength and endurance exercises and L-glutamine supplementation prevented intestinal inflammation and improved cytokines and oxidative stress levels without altering gastric dysmotility in rats with UC.

explanation.what_it_is_line: An amino acid (protein building block) your body makes and uses for intestinal and immune health.
explanation.what_it_is: L-glutamine is one of 20 amino acids — the molecules your cells chain together to build and repair proteins. Your body produces glutamine naturally, but under stress (illness, intense exercise, injury) you may use it faster than you make it. It is sold as a powder or capsule supplement, usually derived from fermented plant or bacterial sources. Glutamine is water-loving (highly polar), meaning it dissolves easily and doesn't linger in fatty tissues.
explanation.how_it_works_line: Fuels gut cells, supports immune function, and may reduce intestinal inflammation and leakiness.
explanation.how_it_works: Glutamine is the preferred fuel for the cells that line your intestines (enterocytes) and for immune cells like lymphocytes. When you take glutamine, your gut absorbs it and these cells use it to generate energy and rebuild their structure. It also appears to strengthen the tight junctions — the seals between intestinal cells — which may reduce unwanted passage of bacteria or toxins into the bloodstream (sometimes called 'leaky gut'). Additionally, glutamine may dampen overactive inflammatory signaling by shifting immune cells away from pro-inflammatory states. The exact molecular pathways are not fully established in humans, but animal studies suggest it works via nutrient sensing pathways and by supporting glutathione (a cellular antioxidant) production.
explanation.safety_line: Well tolerated in short-term trials; long-term safety and effects in vulnerable groups remain untested.
explanation.safety_detail: Short-term supplementation (days to weeks) at oral doses up to 40 g/day has been associated with minimal reported side effects in the human trials retrieved — mostly mild gastrointestinal symptoms at higher doses. However, retrieved trials were generally brief and involved mostly healthy adults or specific disease cohorts (cystic fibrosis, sickle cell disease, cancer); duration and population coverage are limited.
safety_bullets: Pregnancy and lactation: not studied in retrieved trials; long-term fetal or infant exposure unknown.
Kidney or liver disease: one observational study (n=10) tracked renal parameters but adequately powered safety data are absent from records.
Drug interactions: not systematically evaluated; potential interactions with immunosuppressants or chemotherapy agents are not documented in retrieved abstracts.
Adolescents and children: only scattered mentions in cancer/cystic fibrosis contexts; pediatric safety profile unconfirmed.
explanation.chem_meaning: Glutamine is a small, water-soluble molecule (molecular weight 146.14) with a strong negative lipophilicity (XLogP −3.1), meaning it cannot cross cell membranes passively and must be transported via amino-acid pumps. This makes it highly available in the bloodstream and gut lumen but prevents it from accumulating in fat stores; it is efficiently cleared via renal excretion or cellular uptake.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Five human RCTs and clinical trials show that oral glutamine supplementation alters gut microbiota composition in obese/overweight adults (2015), improves gastrointestinal tolerance at escalating doses in healthy volunteers (2020), and reduces intestinal complications in cancer patients (2001, 2025, 2023). Seventeen animal studies further demonstrate that glutamine supports enteric nervous-system health and reduces gastrointestinal permeability. Verified sample sizes across seven studies total ~699 participants, though many abstracts omit sample size, indicating the full cohort is larger. Most trials lasted weeks to months.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Multiple human RCTs exist with consistent directional findings, but no pooled meta-analysis across studies has confirmed uniform agreement on effect size or mechanism. Precision is moderate due to incomplete sample-size reporting and heterogeneous populations (healthy, obese, cancer).

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Nine human trials (RCTs and observational studies) report that glutamine supplementation reduces inflammatory markers and improves clinical outcomes in diverse populations: sickle-cell disease (2026, n=53), strength/glycemia in mixed exercise cohorts (2021), combined-exercise training on oral redox balance (2020), cystic fibrosis (2016), and radiation-induced oral mucositis in cancer patients (2026, n=84). Sixteen animal studies support immune and anti-inflammatory effects. Verified participants across eight studies: ~2657, though full total likely higher due to missing sample-size data.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Solid human evidence across multiple disease contexts and healthy populations, but lack of a unified meta-analysis and inconsistency in effect magnitude and mechanism across trials keeps this at Moderate.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Four human studies (RCTs and observational) show that glutamine maintains or improves immune markers in healthy adults (2020, n size unreported) and in clinical populations including cystic fibrosis (2016), cancer patients (2001, n=13), and surgical cancer patients receiving parenteral glutamine (2021, n=1950, observational). Five animal studies report reduced gastrointestinal permeability, enhanced immune status in weaned piglets, and stress-biomarker reductions. Verified human participants: ~2233, though abstracts often lack explicit sample sizes.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Promising human RCTs and observational data exist, but sample sizes are unconfirmed in most abstracts, heterogeneity across populations is significant, and no meta-analysis binds the findings together.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Five human studies (mostly RCTs) show that oral glutamine supplementation enhances knee extensor/flexor strength and power (2021), reduces muscle soreness and damage markers after knee surgery (2015) and in professional basketball (2021), and improves strength recovery in surgical settings (2018, systematic review). One animal study (2021) examined glutamine plus exercise on immune and inflammation outcomes. Sample sizes could not be verified from abstracts for most trials, and the 2018 systematic review is the only independent aggregation of data.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Several human RCTs show consistent strength gains, but individual sample sizes are largely unreported, and the conclusion rests primarily on a single systematic review not independently replicated in the retrieved records.

explanation.evidence_base: Evidence is predominantly human — 23 human trials (RCTs, clinical trials, and observational studies) versus 39 animal studies across all four outcomes. Most human data is recent (2015–2026), with RCTs concentrated in specific populations: cancer, cystic fibrosis, sickle-cell disease, and healthy exercisers. Verified participant counts are large (~2000–2600 per outcome where data exist), but many trial abstracts omit sample size, so true totals are likely substantially higher. The absence of formal meta-analyses and the heterogeneity of populations and study designs limits confidence to Moderate across all outcomes.
explanation.open_questions: The retrieved records do not show studies in pregnant women, infants, or children outside cancer/cystic-fibrosis contexts; safety in those groups remains untested. Long-term supplementation (>3 months) is sparsely represented; most trials last weeks to a few months. Mechanism-of-action studies in humans are rare — most mechanistic detail comes from animal models and cell studies, so whether the same pathways drive effects in people is an open question. The records include only a sample (~40 abstracts per outcome); do not claim the full published literature is small or understudied — only that these records show a moderate evidence base with these specific gaps.

appraisal.headline: No pooled meta-analysis exists for any outcome; most individual studies lack reported sample sizes, making it impossible to assess whether the observed effects are real or driven by publication bias and heterogeneous, small trials.

concerns.issue: Absence of pooled analysis; unverified consistency
concerns.detail: Across all four outcomes (gut, inflammation, immune, muscle), the engine explicitly notes 'no pooled analysis confirms they agree' and consistency is 'held at moderate pending review.' For gut/digestion and inflammation, abstracts report only 7 of 22 and 8 of 25 studies respectively—meaning ~70% lack sample sizes. Without meta-analysis and with widespread missing data, the true effect size and heterogeneity cannot be determined. A single large outlier study could reverse the narrative.

concerns.issue: Heavy reliance on animal models with unclear translatability
concerns.detail: Human studies comprise only 5 of 22 (gut), 9 of 25 (inflammation), and 4 of 9 (immune) trials. Animal studies (17, 16, and 5 respectively) dominate the evidence base. Animal gut physiology, microbial composition, and immune response differ substantially from humans, yet no mechanism-of-action bridge links rodent/swine outcomes to human clinical benefit. The inflammation and immune outcomes rest partly on animal intestinal permeability and biomarker studies (e.g., 2023 animal study on GI permeability) with no human confirmation.

concerns.issue: Majority of human trials are very small and lack transparency on sample size
concerns.detail: Among human RCTs and clinical trials with reported n, median is 30–32 (gut/digestion and inflammation). Three RCTs are reported: two with n=13 and n=30 (both very small), one 2020 trial with unreported n, and one 2016 cystic fibrosis trial with unreported n. For muscle strength, sample sizes are completely unextractable from abstracts. Small trials are vulnerable to random error, measurement bias, and selective reporting—especially problematic when no pooled analysis corrects for these issues.

concerns.issue: Heterogeneous populations and indications without stratified analysis
concerns.detail: Trials span cancer patients, cystic fibrosis, sickle cell disease, pancreatic cancer, obese/overweight adults, and healthy athletes. The 2016 CF trial, 2023 pancreatic cancer trial, and 2026 sickle cell trial (GLOBE, n=53) are mechanistically distinct contexts. No subgroup analysis or sensitivity analysis is documented. Pooling across such disparate populations without stratification could obscure condition-specific effects or hide net-zero effects in the healthy population.

concerns.issue: Observational and unclassified study designs inflating precision numerically
concerns.detail: The inflammation and immune outcomes include observational (e.g., 2021 n=1950 parenteral supplementation in surgical cancer patients) and unclassified designs (e.g., 2023 'Stratification of β<sup>S</sup>β<sup>+</sup> Compound Heterozygotes'). These designs lack randomization and blinding. The large n=1950 observational study may inflate the precision count, but observational data on parenteral glutamine (administered in hospitals) cannot support inference about oral supplement efficacy in outpatient settings. Mixing designs without weighting by rigor inflates false confidence.

concerns.issue: Recency bias and incomplete outcome reporting
concerns.detail: Several 2025–2026 trials are listed but only as titles/abstracts; full results are unavailable for verification. Older studies (2001, 2013–2016) have limited transparency by modern standards. The 2020 'Gastrointestinal Tolerance' trial appears in both gut and immune outcomes but with no sample size reported, suggesting possible selective outcome reporting or endpoint multiplicity without preregistration data visible in these records.

appraisal.mechanism_check: The plausible mechanism—glutamine as a fuel for enterocytes and immune cells, and as a precursor for glutathione and tight-junction proteins—is biochemically sound. However, the leap from cell culture and animal intestinal physiology to human clinical outcomes (reduced inflammation, improved muscle strength, enhanced immunity) is substantial. In vitro bactericidal effects (2023 gentamicin study) and rodent intestinal permeability (2023 animal study) do not confirm that oral glutamine supplementation achieves sufficient luminal or systemic concentration in humans to replicate those effects. The heterogeneity of study populations (cancer, CF, sickle cell, athletes, healthy obese adults) suggests the mechanism may be context-dependent, yet no trial stratifies by baseline glutamine status, disease severity, or renal/hepatic function—all of which would affect bioavailability.
appraisal.strongest_counterargument: A skeptic would argue: (1) No meta-analysis exists, so the apparent consensus is an illusion created by listing many small, heterogeneous trials without a common effect estimate. (2) Most human RCTs are under 35 participants and lack preregistered primary outcomes; any effect could be noise or p-hacking. (3) The observational n=1950 study uses parenteral (IV) glutamine in post-surgical cancer patients—a completely different route and population from oral supplementation in healthy or chronically ill outpatients. (4) Animal studies (70% of the base) cannot be assumed to predict human response, especially given that glutamine is conditionally essential and requirements vary by disease state. The Moderate grade reflects genuine uncertainty, not genuine confidence.
appraisal.what_would_change_the_picture: A properly powered (n≥200 per arm), preregistered, double-blind RCT in a single, well-defined population (e.g., post-surgical patients, cystic fibrosis, or healthy adults) with a primary endpoint assessed by an independent blinded evaluator, combined with a prospective meta-analysis of all existing small trials, would establish whether the effect is real or an artifact of publication bias. Mechanistic studies linking oral bioavailability (pharmacokinetics) and tissue glutamine concentrations to clinical outcomes in humans would close the animal-to-human translatability gap.

explanation_es.what_it_is_line: Un aminoácido (bloque constructor de proteínas) que tu cuerpo produce y utiliza para la salud intestinal e inmunológica.
explanation_es.what_it_is: La L-glutamina es uno de 20 aminoácidos — las moléculas que tus células encadenan para construir y reparar proteínas. Tu cuerpo produce glutamina de forma natural, pero bajo estrés (enfermedad, ejercicio intenso, lesión) podrías usarla más rápido de lo que la produces. Se vende como suplemento en polvo o cápsula, generalmente derivado de fuentes vegetales fermentadas o bacterianas. La glutamina ama el agua (altamente polar), lo que significa que se disuelve fácilmente y no se acumula en los tejidos grasosos.
explanation_es.how_it_works_line: Alimenta las células intestinales, respalda la función inmunológica, y puede reducir la inflamación intestinal y la permeabilidad.
explanation_es.how_it_works: La glutamina es el combustible preferido de las células que revisten tus intestinos (enterocitos) y de las células inmunológicas como los linfocitos. Cuando tomas glutamina, tu intestino la absorbe y estas células la usan para generar energía y reconstruir su estructura. También parece fortalecer las uniones estrechas — los sellos entre las células intestinales — lo que puede reducir el paso no deseado de bacterias o toxinas hacia el torrente sanguíneo (a veces llamado 'intestino permeable'). Además, la glutamina puede disminuir la señalización inflamatoria excesiva al desplazar las células inmunológicas lejos de estados proinflamatorios. Las vías moleculares exactas no están completamente establecidas en humanos, pero los estudios en animales sugieren que funciona a través de vías de detección de nutrientes y al apoyar la producción de glutatión (un antioxidante celular).
explanation_es.safety_line: Bien tolerada en ensayos a corto plazo; la seguridad a largo plazo y los efectos en grupos vulnerables siguen sin ser evaluados.
explanation_es.safety_detail: La suplementación a corto plazo (días a semanas) a dosis orales de hasta 40 g/día se ha asociado con efectos adversos mínimos reportados en los ensayos humanos recuperados — principalmente síntomas gastrointestinales leves a dosis más altas. Sin embargo, los ensayos recuperados fueron generalmente breves e involucraron principalmente adultos sanos o cohortes de enfermedades específicas (fibrosis quística, enfermedad de células falciformes, cáncer); la duración y cobertura de población son limitadas.
safety_bullets: Embarazo y lactancia: no estudiado en ensayos recuperados; la exposición fetal o infantil a largo plazo es desconocida.
Enfermedad renal o hepática: un estudio observacional (n=10) rastreó parámetros renales pero faltan datos de seguridad adecuadamente potenciados en los registros.
Interacciones farmacológicas: no evaluadas sistemáticamente; las posibles interacciones con inmunosupresores o agentes de quimioterapia no están documentadas en los resúmenes recuperados.
Adolescentes y niños: solo menciones dispersas en contextos de cáncer/fibrosis quística; el perfil de seguridad pediátrica no está confirmado.
explanation_es.chem_meaning: La glutamina es una molécula pequeña, soluble en agua (peso molecular 146.14) con una fuerte lipofilia negativa (XLogP −3.1), lo que significa que no puede atravesar pasivamente las membranas celulares y debe ser transportada a través de bombas de aminoácidos. Esto la hace altamente disponible en el torrente sanguíneo y en la luz intestinal pero evita que se acumule en los depósitos de grasa; se elimina eficientemente a través de la excreción renal o la captación celular.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Cinco ensayos clínicos y RCTs humanos muestran que la suplementación oral de glutamina altera la composición de la microbiota intestinal en adultos obesos/con sobrepeso (2015), mejora la tolerancia gastrointestinal en dosis escalonadas en voluntarios sanos (2020), y reduce complicaciones intestinales en pacientes con cáncer (2001, 2025, 2023). Diecisiete estudios en animales demuestran además que la glutamina respalda la salud del sistema nervioso entérico y reduce la permeabilidad gastrointestinal. Los tamaños de muestra verificados en siete estudios totalizan aproximadamente 699 participantes, aunque muchos resúmenes omiten el tamaño de la muestra, lo que indica que la cohorte completa es más grande. La mayoría de los ensayos duraron semanas a meses.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Existen múltiples RCTs humanos con hallazgos direccionales consistentes, pero ningún metanálisis agrupado entre estudios ha confirmado acuerdo uniforme sobre el tamaño del efecto o el mecanismo. La precisión es moderada debido al reporte incompleto del tamaño de la muestra y poblaciones heterogéneas (sana, obesa, cáncer).

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Nueve ensayos humanos (RCTs y estudios observacionales) reportan que la suplementación de glutamina reduce marcadores inflamatorios y mejora los resultados clínicos en poblaciones diversas: enfermedad de células falciformes (2026, n=53), fuerza/glucemia en cohortes de ejercicio mixto (2021), entrenamiento de ejercicio combinado en balance redox oral (2020), fibrosis quística (2016), y mucositis oral inducida por radiación en pacientes con cáncer (2026, n=84). Dieciséis estudios en animales respaldan efectos inmunológicos y antiinflamatorios. Participantes verificados en ocho estudios: aproximadamente 2657, aunque el total completo probablemente sea mayor debido a datos de tamaño de muestra faltantes.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Evidencia humana sólida en múltiples contextos de enfermedad y poblaciones sanas, pero la falta de un metanálisis unificado e inconsistencia en la magnitud del efecto y el mecanismo entre ensayos mantiene esto en Moderada.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Cuatro estudios humanos (RCTs y observacionales) muestran que la glutamina mantiene o mejora marcadores inmunológicos en adultos sanos (2020, tamaño n no reportado) y en poblaciones clínicas que incluyen fibrosis quística (2016), pacientes con cáncer (2001, n=13), y pacientes con cáncer quirúrgico que reciben glutamina parenteral (2021, n=1950, observacional). Cinco estudios en animales reportan permeabilidad gastrointestinal reducida, estado inmunológico mejorado en lechones destetados, y reducciones de marcadores de estrés. Participantes humanos verificados: aproximadamente 2233, aunque los resúmenes frecuentemente carecen de tamaños de muestra explícitos.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Existen RCTs humanos prometedores y datos observacionales, pero los tamaños de muestra no están confirmados en la mayoría de los resúmenes, la heterogeneidad entre poblaciones es significativa, y ningún metanálisis vincula los hallazgos juntos.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Cinco estudios humanos (principalmente RCTs) muestran que la suplementación oral de glutamina mejora la fuerza y potencia de los extensores/flexores de rodilla (2021), reduce el dolor muscular y marcadores de daño después de cirugía de rodilla (2015) y en baloncesto profesional (2021), y mejora la recuperación de fuerza en entornos quirúrgicos (2018, revisión sistemática). Un estudio en animales (2021) examinó glutamina más ejercicio en resultados de inmunidad e inflamación. Los tamaños de muestra no pudieron ser verificados a partir de los resúmenes para la mayoría de los ensayos, y la revisión sistemática de 2018 es la única agregación independiente de datos.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Varios RCTs humanos muestran ganancias de fuerza consistentes, pero los tamaños de muestra individuales en su mayoría no se reportan, y la conclusión descansa principalmente en una única revisión sistemática no replicada independientemente en los registros recuperados.

explanation_es.evidence_base: La evidencia es predominantemente humana — 23 ensayos humanos (RCTs, ensayos clínicos y estudios observacionales) versus 39 estudios en animales en los cuatro resultados. La mayoría de los datos humanos son recientes (2015–2026), con RCTs concentrados en poblaciones específicas: cáncer, fibrosis quística, enfermedad de células falciformes, y ejercitadores sanos. Los recuentos de participantes verificados son grandes (~2000–2600 por resultado donde existen datos), pero muchos resúmenes de ensayos omiten el tamaño de la muestra, por lo que los totales verdaderos probablemente sean sustancialmente mayores. La ausencia de metanálisis formales y la heterogeneidad de poblaciones y diseños de estudio limita la confianza a Moderada en todos los resultados.
explanation_es.open_questions: Los registros recuperados no muestran estudios en mujeres embarazadas, lactantes o niños fuera de contextos de cáncer/fibrosis quística; la seguridad en esos grupos sigue sin ser evaluada. La suplementación a largo plazo (>3 meses) está escasamente representada; la mayoría de los ensayos duran semanas a pocos meses. Los estudios de mecanismo de acción en humanos son raros — la mayoría de los detalles mecanísticos provienen de modelos animales y estudios celulares, por lo que si las mismas vías impulsan efectos en personas es una pregunta abierta. Los registros incluyen solo una muestra (~40 resúmenes por resultado); no afirmes que la literatura publicada completa es pequeña o poco estudiada — solo que estos registros muestran una base de evidencia moderada con estas brechas específicas.

appraisal_es.headline: No existe metanálisis agrupado para ningún resultado; la mayoría de estudios individuales carecen de tamaños de muestra reportados, lo que hace imposible evaluar si los efectos observados son reales o están impulsados por sesgo de publicación y ensayos heterogéneos y pequeños.

concerns.issue: Ausencia de análisis agrupado; consistencia no verificada
concerns.detail: En los cuatro resultados (intestinal, inflamación, inmunidad, músculo), el motor explícitamente señala 'sin análisis agrupado que confirme su concordancia' y la consistencia se 'mantiene como moderada pendiente de revisión.' Para los resultados intestinales/digestivos e inflamación, los resúmenes reportan solo 7 de 22 y 8 de 25 estudios respectivamente—lo que significa que ~70% carecen de tamaños de muestra. Sin metanálisis y con datos faltantes generalizados, el verdadero tamaño del efecto y la heterogeneidad no pueden determinarse. Un único estudio atípico grande podría invertir la narrativa.

concerns.issue: Fuerte dependencia de modelos animales con translatibilidad poco clara
concerns.detail: Los estudios en humanos comprenden solo 5 de 22 (intestinal), 9 de 25 (inflamación), y 4 de 9 (inmunidad) ensayos. Los estudios animales (17, 16, y 5 respectivamente) dominan la base de evidencia. La fisiología intestinal animal, la composición microbiana, y la respuesta inmunológica difieren sustancialmente de los humanos, pero ningún puente de mecanismo de acción vincula los resultados en roedores/cerdos con el beneficio clínico en humanos. Los resultados de inflamación e inmunidad se basan parcialmente en estudios de permeabilidad intestinal animal y biomarcadores (p. ej., estudio animal 2023 sobre permeabilidad GI) sin confirmación en humanos.

concerns.issue: La mayoría de ensayos en humanos son muy pequeños y carecen de transparencia sobre tamaño de muestra
concerns.detail: Entre ensayos clínicos RCT y clínicos en humanos con n reportado, la mediana es 30–32 (intestinal/digestión e inflamación). Se reportan tres RCT: dos con n=13 y n=30 (ambos muy pequeños), un ensayo 2020 con n no reportado, y un ensayo 2016 de fibrosis quística con n no reportado. Para fuerza muscular, los tamaños de muestra son completamente no extractables de los resúmenes. Los ensayos pequeños son vulnerables a error aleatorio, sesgo de medición, e informe selectivo—especialmente problemático cuando ningún análisis agrupado corrige estos problemas.

concerns.issue: Poblaciones e indicaciones heterogéneas sin análisis estratificado
concerns.detail: Los ensayos abarcan pacientes con cáncer, fibrosis quística, enfermedad de células falciformes, cáncer pancreático, adultos obesos/con sobrepeso, y atletas sanos. El ensayo CF 2016, el ensayo de cáncer pancreático 2023, y el ensayo de células falciformes 2026 (GLOBE, n=53) son contextos mecanísticamente distintos. No se documenta análisis de subgrupos ni análisis de sensibilidad. Agrupar poblaciones tan dispares sin estratificación podría oscurecer efectos específicos de la condición u ocultar efectos netos cero en la población sana.

concerns.issue: Diseños de estudios observacionales y no clasificados inflando precisión numéricamente
concerns.detail: Los resultados de inflamación e inmunidad incluyen diseños observacionales (p. ej., suplementación parenteral 2021 n=1950 en pacientes quirúrgicos con cáncer) y diseños no clasificados (p. ej., 'Estratificación de Heterocigotos Compuestos β<sup>S</sup>β<sup>+</sup>' 2023). Estos diseños carecen de randomización y enmascaramiento. El gran estudio observacional n=1950 puede inflar el recuento de precisión, pero datos observacionales sobre glutamina parenteral (administrada en hospitales) no pueden respaldar inferencia sobre eficacia de suplementos orales en ambientes ambulatorios. Mezclar diseños sin ponderación por rigor infla confianza falsa.

concerns.issue: Sesgo de recencia e informe incompleto de resultados
concerns.detail: Varios ensayos 2025–2026 se listan pero solo como títulos/resúmenes; los resultados completos no están disponibles para verificación. Los estudios más antiguos (2001, 2013–2016) tienen transparencia limitada por estándares modernos. El ensayo 'Tolerancia Gastrointestinal' 2020 aparece tanto en resultados intestinales como inmunológicos pero sin tamaño de muestra reportado, sugiriendo posible informe selectivo de resultados o multiplicidad de endpoints sin datos de preregistro visibles en estos registros.

appraisal_es.mechanism_check: El mecanismo plausible—glutamina como combustible para enterocitos y células inmunológicas, y como precursor para glutatión y proteínas de uniones estrechas—es bioquímicamente sólido. Sin embargo, el salto de fisiología intestinal de cultivo celular y animal a resultados clínicos en humanos (inflamación reducida, fortaleza muscular mejorada, inmunidad mejorada) es sustancial. Los efectos bactericidas in vitro (estudio de gentamicina 2023) y la permeabilidad intestinal en roedores (estudio animal 2023) no confirman que la suplementación oral de glutamina alcance concentración luminal o sistémica suficiente en humanos para replicar esos efectos. La heterogeneidad de poblaciones de estudio (cáncer, FC, células falciformes, atletas, adultos obesos sanos) sugiere el mecanismo podría ser dependiente del contexto, pero ningún ensayo estratifica por estado de glutamina basal, severidad de la enfermedad, o función renal/hepática—todos los cuales afectarían la biodisponibilidad.
appraisal_es.strongest_counterargument: Un escéptico argumentaría: (1) No existe metanálisis, así que el aparente consenso es una ilusión creada por listar muchos ensayos pequeños y heterogéneos sin un estimador de efecto común. (2) La mayoría de RCT en humanos tienen menos de 35 participantes y carecen de resultados primarios preregistrados; cualquier efecto podría ser ruido o p-hacking. (3) El estudio observacional n=1950 usa glutamina parenteral (IV) en pacientes quirúrgicos con cáncer—una ruta y población completamente diferentes de suplementación oral en pacientes ambulatorios sanos o crónicamente enfermos. (4) Los estudios animales (70% de la base) no pueden asumirse que predicen respuesta humana, especialmente dado que glutamina es condicionalmente esencial y los requisitos varían por estado de enfermedad. La calificación Moderada refleja incertidumbre genuina, no confianza genuina.
appraisal_es.what_would_change_the_picture: Un RCT doble ciego adecuadamente potenciado (n≥200 por brazo), preregistrado, en una población única bien definida (p. ej., pacientes post-quirúrgicos, fibrosis quística, o adultos sanos) con un resultado primario evaluado por un evaluador ciego independiente, combinado con un metanálisis prospectivo de todos los ensayos pequeños existentes, establecería si el efecto es real o un artefacto del sesgo de publicación. Estudios mecanísticos vinculando biodisponibilidad oral (farmacocinética) y concentraciones de glutamina tisular a resultados clínicos en humanos cerraría la brecha de translatibilidad animal-a-humano.
